Module 1: Getting Started with Python

1.1 Introduction to Python

Python Introduction

Welcome to the world of coding! 🚀
You are about to learn Python—one of the most popular, creative, and beginner-friendly programming languages on the planet.
Think of programming as giving superpowers to your computer. Just like you use English or Hindi to talk to your friends, you use Python to tell your computer, phone, or robot exactly what to do.
You do not need to write any code on this page. Just get ready for an exciting adventure!
When you're ready, click Next Lesson to discover what makes Python so special.
Features of Python
Why do millions of young creators choose Python? Here are four reasons:
Reads Like Plain English: Python code is clean and simple. You don't have to memorize strange, confusing symbols.
Super Versatile: You can use Python to build games, craft websites, analyze space data, or create smart AI bots.
Beginner-Friendly: Python gives friendly clues when you make a mistake, helping you fix your code quickly.
Works Everywhere: A Python program written on Windows runs smoothly on a Mac, Linux, or even a tiny mini-computer like a Raspberry Pi.
Click Next Lesson to see what real-world things you can build with Python!
Why Python?
Python isn't just for learning—it powers some of the coolest tools and games in the world!
Video Games: Game developers use Python to script mechanics and design characters.
Space Exploration: NASA and rocket scientists use Python to track satellites and study distant planets.
Entertainment: Platforms like YouTube, Netflix, and Spotify use Python to stream your favorite videos and suggest music.
Artificial Intelligence (AI): Python is the #1 language used to teach computers how to recognize faces, drive autonomous cars, and chat like real people.
If you can imagine it, you can build it with Python!
Click Next Lesson to see how a computer actually runs your code.
How Python programs execute
Have you ever wondered what happens after you click the Run button?
Computers do not speak human languages. They only understand 0s and 1s. That's where the Python Interpreter comes in!
You write the code in the code editor (e.g., in simple English words).
The Interpreter translates it: Python reads your instructions line by line, from top to bottom, like reading a comic book.
The Computer executes it: Your computer follows the instructions instantly and displays the result on your screen
Figure: Code Editor (print) ---> Python Interpreter (Translator) ---> Console Screen
Now that you know how it works behind the scenes, let's write your first command! Click Next Lesson.
The print() function
To make your computer speak or show a message on the screen, Python gives you a special command called the print() function.
Whatever you place inside the parentheses ( ) and quotation marks " " will be displayed in the output console.
All you need to do is click the Run Code button.
How It Works:
print: The name of the Python action (always in lowercase).
( ) Parentheses: The container that holds what you want to show.
" " Quotation Marks: Tell Python that this is literal text (called a string), so Python prints it exactly as typed, without the quotes.
Figure: Print Hey Welcome to Y Coders
Be Careful:
Python is case-sensitive!
print("Hey") is correct.
Print("Hey") with a capital P will cause a NameError because Python doesn't recognize it.
Click Next Lesson to learn how to leave secret notes in your code.
Comments (#) & Code Readability
As your programs grow, you'll want to add notes to remind yourself—or your teammates—what your code does. In Python, these notes are called comments.
To create a comment, start the line with the # symbol (hash / pound sign):
Output
Why Comments Matter:
Python completely ignores anything that comes after #. It will never appear on the output screen.
Comments make your code clean, readable, and easy to understand when you come back to it next week.
Click Next Lesson to test your knowledge with a quick quiz!
Quiz: Displaying Messages
Which of the following lines of code will successfully display Welcome, Gamer! on the screen?
Tap an option below to answer:
Practice: Your First Python Program
Problem Description

You are setting up the control console for a brand-new space explorer robot. Write a Python program that greets the crew with the exact message:
Mission Control: All systems ready!
Instructions & Hints:
Use the print() function with lowercase letters.
Put parentheses ( ) right after print.

Make sure your spelling, punctuation, and spaces match the expected output.
Example:
Quiz: Spot the Comment
What will be displayed on the screen when this code runs?
Tap an option below to answer:

A: Level 1 Completed! followed by Starting Level 2...
Incorrect, give it another shot!
The first line begins with #, which makes it a comment. Python completely ignores it.

B: Starting Level 2...
Correct Answer! 🎉
Because the first line starts with #, Python skips it completely and only runs the second line.

C: # print("Level 1 Completed!")
Incorrect, give it another shot!
Comments are never printed to the screen. They are invisible notes for human coders.

D: An error occurs.
Incorrect, give it another shot!
The code is 100% valid Python. Commenting out code is a normal and useful feature.
Chapter Review
Congratulations! 🏆
You've officially written and understood your first Python programs!
Figure: Course Flow
Here is a quick recap of the superpowers you unlocked in Chapter 1:
Python: A friendly, powerful coding language that reads like plain English.
Interpreter: Reads your code line by line from top to bottom and runs it.
print("message"): The command to display text on the screen. Always remember lowercase print, parentheses (), and quotation marks "".
Comments (#): Notes for humans that Python ignores. Use them to make your code neat and easy to understand.
Ready for Chapter 2? In the next chapter, we'll dive into Data Types & Variables and learn how computers remember game scores and player names!

1.2 Displaying Output

Output Intro

Welcome to your next coding level! 🎮

In programming, output is everything your computer displays back to you on the screen—like a high score, a game dialogue, or a mission alert.

So far, you’ve displayed simple greetings. In this chapter, you’ll unlock real console mastery: formatting messages cleanly, printing numbers alongside words, handling line breaks, and using Python’s superpower: f-strings!

No code needed on this page. Click Next Lesson to get started!

Printing Numbers & Text

Python treats plain words and pure numbers differently:

Text (Strings): Must always be wrapped in quotation marks " ".

Numbers: Can be printed directly without quotes!

Output

Why This Matters

When you put numbers in quotes like "100", Python sees them as plain letters (like a sticker). When you write 100 without quotes, Python recognizes it as a real number you can calculate with!

Click Next Lesson to discover how to write longer stories across multiple lines.

Multiline Strings

What if you want to print a long poem, a character speech, or ASCII banner art without writing print() ten times?

Python gives you a special trick: Triple Quotes (""" or ''').

Output

Anything inside """ keeps its exact layout—including every enter, blank line, and space!

Click Next Lesson to test this out with a quiz.

Quiz: Multiline Strings

Which symbol allows you to write a single string that spans across multiple lines?

Tap an option below to answer:

A: """ (Triple quotes)

Correct Answer! 🎉
Wrapping text between triple quotes """ or ''' lets you write across multiple lines freely.

B: // (Double forward slash)

Incorrect, give it another shot!
In Python, // is an arithmetic division operator, not a text symbol.

C: ### (Triple hash)

Incorrect, give it another shot!
A hash symbol # creates comments, which Python ignores completely.

D: (( )) (Double parentheses)

Incorrect, give it another shot!
Parentheses group instructions; they do not create multiline text.

Practice: Multiline Quest Notice

Problem Description

You are making an adventure game. Use a single print() statement with triple quotes to display this quest notice board:

Plaintext

Hints:

Write print(""" on the top.

Type the three lines exactly as shown.

Close the message with """).

Example:

Print Multiple Values

You don’t have to create separate print() lines for every item. You can display multiple values inside a single print() by separating them with a comma ,.

Output

How It Works:

Every time Python sees a comma , inside print(), it automatically adds a single space between the items. You can mix words and numbers freely!

Click Next Lesson to test your eye on commas!

Quiz: The Comma Separator

What will be displayed on the screen when this code runs?

Tap an option below to answer:

A: Apples:5Coins:20

Incorrect, give it another shot!
Python automatically adds a single space between items separated by commas.

B: Apples: 5 Coins: 20

Correct Answer! 🎉
The commas place a neat space between each word and number.

C: Apples: ,5, Coins: ,20

Incorrect, give it another shot!
The commas inside print() act as separators; they do not appear on screen.

D: An error occurs.

Incorrect, give it another shot!
Passing multiple arguments separated by commas is standard, valid Python.

Practice: Race Track Scoreboard

Problem Description

Write a program that uses a single print() function to display a race car's position and speed in one line:
Car: 7   Speed: 180

Hints:

Use one print() statement.

Pass four items separated by commas: "Car:", 7, "Speed:", and 180.

Put quotation marks only on text, not on the numbers.

Example:

Print Newline (\n)

Want your output to drop down to the next line without writing multiple print() commands? Use the magic escape code: \n (newline).

Think of \n like pressing the Enter key on your keyboard right in the middle of your sentence!

Output

Click Next Lesson for a quick check!

Quiz: Newline Mystery

What will be the output of the following line?

Tap an option below to answer:

A: Red Blue Green on one line

Incorrect, give it another shot!
\n doesn't insert a space; it pushes the next word to a brand-new line.

B: Red\nBlue\nGreen

Incorrect, give it another shot!
Python treats \n as an action command, not ordinary text letters.

C: Three lines with Red, then Blue, then Green

Correct Answer! 🎉
Each \n acts like pressing Enter, splitting the three colors onto their own lines.

D: An error occurs.

Incorrect, give it another shot!
\n is a completely valid escape sequence in Python.

Practice: Detective Badge

Problem Description

Using only one print() statement and the newline character \n, display the following badge on two separate lines:

Line 1: Detective: Sherlock

Line 2: Case: The Stolen Gem

Hints:

Write "Detective: Sherlock\nCase: The Stolen Gem" inside print().

Do not leave spaces immediately around \n unless you want extra indentation.

Example:

Common Errors When Printing

Every coder runs into bugs—here are 3 common ones to watch out for:

1. Forgetting the Comma:

Fix: Put a comma , between different values: print("Coins:", 50).

2. Mixing Up Slashes:

Fix: Always use backslash \n, not forward slash /n.

3. Mismatched Quotes:

Fix: Match double quotes with double quotes "..." or single with single '...'.

Click Next Lesson to see how we print variables!

Print Strings & Variables

In programming, a variable is like a labeled toy box that holds a value (like a score or a pet’s name).

You can combine a descriptive text label with a variable using a comma ,:

Output

Notice that the label "My dog:" is in quotes because it’s text, but pet_name is not in quotes so Python looks inside the box to find "Bolt"!

Quiz: Quotes or No Quotes?

Look at this code:

What will appear on the screen?

Tap an option below to answer:

A: SuperNova on both lines

Incorrect, give it another shot!
The first print("hero") has quotes, so it prints the word hero.

B: hero followed by SuperNova

Correct Answer! 🎉
"hero" prints literal letters. hero without quotes retrieves the value stored inside the variable.

C: hero on both lines

Incorrect, give it another shot!
The second print(hero) accesses the variable's value, which is SuperNova.

D: An error occurs on line 2.

Incorrect, give it another shot!
Both statements are completely valid Python.

Practice: Space Cadet ID

Problem Description

Create two variables:

cadet_name with the value "Astra"

rank with the value 1

Then, print them using two separate print() statements to match the expected output.

Hints:

print("Cadet:", cadet_name)

print("Rank:", rank)

Example:

Practice: Wizard Inventory

Problem Description

Create three variables:

spell with the value "Freeze"

potions with the value 3

power with the value 9.8

Use a single print() statement to display all three values with labels in one row:
Spell: Freeze Potions: 3 Power: 9.8

Example:

Python f-strings

While commas work fine, Python has a much cooler and cleaner way to mix variables and text: f-strings (formatted strings)!

To use an f-string:

Put the letter f right before the quotation mark.

Put any variable name inside curly braces { }.

Output

Python automatically replaces {character} with "Pikachu" and {hp} with 120. It reads like a complete, natural sentence!

Click Next Lesson to see how to save formatted text into a new variable!

New Variables Using f-strings

You don’t have to print an f-string right away. You can store the formatted result inside a brand-new variable and use it whenever you need!

Output

Here, the variable forecast now stores the combined sentence. This is super helpful for building automated notifications and game dialogues!

Quiz: Spot the f-string Bug

What is the output of the following code?

Tap an option below to answer:

A: Your total score is 50
Incorrect, give it another shot! Notice what is missing before the quotation mark: there is no f!

B: Your total score is {score}
Correct Answer! 🎉
Because the letter f was omitted before ", Python treats {score} as normal text instead of evaluating the variable!

C: Your total score is score
Incorrect, give it another shot! Without f, Python prints the curly braces { } literally as typed.

D: A SyntaxError occurs.
Incorrect, give it another shot! Plain text inside quotes with curly braces is legal Python text, so no error is thrown.

Practice: Victory Banner

Problem Description

You are celebrating a game tournament victory!

1. Create a variable winner with the value "Team Alpha".

2. Create a variable trophies with the value 4.

3. Create a new variable named banner using an f-string that formats the message:

Congrats to Team Alpha for winning 4 trophies!

4. Print the banner variable.

Hints:

banner = f"Congrats to {winner} for winning {trophies} trophies!"

print(banner)

1.3 Comments

Introduction to Comments
Imagine you are doing a science experiment at school and writing notes in your lab notebook. You write down measurements, but you also write short notes to explain what those numbers mean.
In Python, you can do the exact same thing using comments.
Suppose you write this line to record the temperature of a greenhouse:
Output
If you forgot the # symbol and just typed:
Python would get confused and throw a SyntaxError because it tries to run your English notes as code!
Comments allow you to add helpful explanations directly inside your file without affecting how your program works.
Click Next Lesson to see how Python handles comments behind the scenes.
Understanding Python Comments
Whenever the Python interpreter sees the # symbol, it treats everything after it on that line as invisible. It simply skips right past it!
Let's look at a smart baking timer program:
Output
What Happened Here?
Lines 1 and 4 start with #, so Python skips them completely.
In Line 3, Python executes print(25) and ignores # Minutes left to bake.
The comments help anyone reading the recipe code understand what it does, but they never clutter the output screen.
Click Next Lesson to learn the different ways to write comments!
Types of Comments
Coders use comments in three main ways depending on how much they want to explain:
1. Single-Line Comments
The entire line is dedicated to an explanation. It starts with #:
2. Inline Comments
A quick note placed at the end of an active line of code:
3. Multi-Line Notes
When you have a longer explanation, you can put a # at the start of each line:
Click Next Lesson to test your knowledge with a quiz!
Quiz: Identifying Comments
A student wrote a program to track a Mars rover. Which of the following lines will be completely ignored by Python when the program runs?
Tap an option below to answer:
A: print("Signal status: Connected")
Incorrect, give it another shot! This is a valid print() statement without a leading #, so Python executes it and displays the message.
B: # Transmitting signal to rover

Correct Answer! 🎉
Because the line begins with #, Python treats the entire line as a comment and skips it completely.
Incorrect, give it another shot! 1500 is inside the print() function, so it will be displayed on the screen.
D: Distance in kilometers
Incorrect, give it another shot! While this text is ignored, it is only part of an inline comment, not the entire line.
Quiz: Output Prediction
A marine biologist is logging ocean dolphin sightings with this code:
What will be displayed on the screen?
Tap an option below to answer:
A: All three dolphin pod lines will be printed.
Incorrect, give it another shot! Lines 1 and 3 start with #, which comments them out so they cannot run.
B: Dolphin Pod 2: 12 sightings

Correct Answer! 🎉
Only Line 2 is executable code. Lines 1 and 3 are commented out, so Python ignores them completely.
C: # print("Dolphin Pod 1: 8 sightings")
Incorrect, give it another shot! The # prevents the line from executing or showing up on the output console.
D: A SyntaxError occurs.
Incorrect, give it another shot! "Commenting out" lines of code is a standard technique used by developers to temporarily disable code without deleting it.

1.4 Understanding Variables

Variable Introduction

So far, we have printed fixed numbers and words directly to the screen. But what if you need to remember information and use it later—like a player's score, the temperature of an incubator, or the name of a space probe?

This is where variables come in!

Think of a variable as a labeled storage box. You put a sticky label on the outside (the variable's name) and place an item inside (the value). Whenever your program needs that item, it just looks up the box by its label!

Figure: A labeled box with the label "player_name" holding the card "Leo"

Click Next Lesson to see how to create your first variable box!

Create Variables

Creating a variable in Python is called assignment. You write the variable name, use the equals sign =, and then give it a value:

How It Works:

planet: The name of your variable (the label on the box).

=: The assignment operator. It tells Python: "Take the value on the right and store it inside the box on the left."

"Mars": The data being stored.

Python stores this information in memory instantly.

Click Next Lesson for a quick check!

Quiz: Spot the Variable

In the following line of code, what is the variable name?

Tap an option below to answer:

A: 120
Incorrect, give it another shot! 120 is the numerical value stored inside the variable, not the variable's name.

B: speed
Correct Answer! 🎉
speed is the label used to identify and store the value in memory.

C: =
Incorrect, give it another shot! The = symbol is the assignment operator used to put the value into the variable.

D: "speed"
Incorrect, give it another shot! Variable names are never written inside quotation marks.

Printing Variables

To see what is stored inside a variable box, pass its name directly to the print() function without quotation marks:

Output

Notice the Difference:

print("dino_name") with quotes prints the literal word dino_name.

print(dino_name) without quotes tells Python to open the box and print T-Rex!

Quiz: Variable vs Text

What will be displayed on the screen when this code runs?

Tap an option below to answer:

A: Falcon on both lines

Incorrect, give it another shot! The first statement has quotes around "animal", so it prints the letters literally.

B: animal followed by Falcon

Correct Answer! 🎉
"animal" prints as plain text, while animal retrieves the stored value "Falcon".

C: animal on both lines

Incorrect, give it another shot! The second statement accesses the variable, which holds "Falcon".

D: A NameError occurs.

Incorrect, give it another shot! Both statements are completely valid Python.

A Common Error: Using Variables Before Creating Them

What happens if you ask Python to open a box that does not exist yet?

Output

Why This Error Happens:

Python reads your code from top to bottom. Because energy_level was never given a value with =, Python has no idea what it is!

How to Fix It:

Always define and assign your variable before you try to print or use it:

Quiz: Identifying the Error

Why does the following code cause an error?

Tap an option below to answer:

A: Variable names cannot store text.
Incorrect, give it another shot! Variables can hold text, numbers, and many other data types.

B: captain is printed before it is created.
Correct Answer! 🎉
Python executes line by line. When line 1 runs, captain has not been created yet, raising a NameError.

C: The word print must be capitalized.
Incorrect, give it another shot! print() must always be lowercase.

D: Missing double quotes around captain in line 2.
Incorrect, give it another shot! Line 2 correctly assigns the string "Aria" to captain.

Practice: Print Variables

Problem Description

You are recording facts about the solar system.

1. Create a variable named highest_mountain and store the string "Olympus Mons".

2. Create a variable named height_km and store the number 21.9.

3. Print highest_mountain on the first line.

4. Print height_km on the second line.

Hints:

Do not put quotes around the variable names inside print().

Keep the text "Olympus Mons" inside quotes, but write the number 21.9 directly.

Example:

Assigning Value (One Variable to Another)

You can copy the value from one variable directly into another variable:

Output

How It Works:

Figure: Assign Value of snack2 to snack1

Quiz: Copying Variables

What is the output of the following code?

Tap an option below to answer:

A: Lemonade
Incorrect, give it another shot! drink1 was updated to drink2's value ("Mango Juice") on line 3.

B: Water
Incorrect, give it another shot! drink2 was changed to "Water" later, but that does not retroactively change drink1.

C: Mango Juice
Correct Answer! 🎉
On line 3, drink1 received a copy of "Mango Juice". Changing drink2 afterward does not affect drink1.

D: An error occurs.
Incorrect, give it another shot! All lines are valid variable assignments.

Practice: Team Captain Handoff

Problem Description

Write a program to transfer a role from one person to another:

1. Create a variable named lead_runner with the value "Kiran".

2. Create a variable named backup_runner with the value "Zoya".

3. Assign the value of backup_runner to lead_runner.

4. Print lead_runner.

Hints:

Use lead_runner = backup_runner to copy the value.

Print lead_runner to verify the new value.

Example:

A Common Error: Assigning Undefined Variables

Look closely at this assignment:

Output

Why This Happens:

In Python, the variable on the right side of = must already exist! You cannot copy data from an empty, non-existent box into another box.

Rule to Remember:

Left side of =: The box you are filling.

Right side of =: The value or existing box you are taking from.

Change Variables

Why are they called variables? Because their values can vary (change) over time!

When you put a new value into an existing variable, the old value is replaced:

Output

The original value 100 is overwritten by 45. A variable only holds one value at a time!

Figure: Change Values Stored in Variable

Quiz: Tracking Variable Updates

What will be displayed at the end of this program?

Tap an option below to answer:

A: 22 28 19
Incorrect, give it another shot! Variables do not remember their full history; only the most recent value is stored.

B: 19
Correct Answer! 🎉
Each assignment overwrites the previous one. The final value stored is 19.

C: 22
Incorrect, give it another shot! 22 was replaced when temperature = 28 executed.

D: 28
Incorrect, give it another shot! 28 was replaced on the next line when temperature = 19 ran.

Practice: Pet Growth Tracker

Problem Description:

Write a program to track a rescue puppy's weight over two months:

1. Create a variable puppy_weight and set it to 4.5.

2. Print puppy_weight.

3. Update puppy_weight to 7.2.

4. Print puppy_weight again.

Example:

Swapping Two Variables

Suppose you have two cups:

Cup A has Orange Juice.

Cup B has Apple Juice.

How do you swap them so Cup A gets Apple Juice and Cup B gets Orange Juice without spilling anything?

You need a third, empty helper cup (temp)!

Here is how you do it in Python:

Output

Without temp, writing cup_a = cup_b directly would overwrite Cup A's original drink, and it would be lost forever!

Figure: Swapping Two Variables

Practice: Swap Backpack Slots

Problem Description

A hiking explorer packed gear in the wrong pockets:

pocket_left = "Compass"

pocket_right = "Water Bottle"

Use a temporary helper variable temp to swap the contents so pocket_left has "Water Bottle" and pocket_right has "Compass". Then print both variables.

Hints:

temp = pocket_left

pocket_left = pocket_right

pocket_right = temp

Scenario-Based Question: Space Station Air Quality

Scenario

An environmental sensor on an international space station logs oxygen levels.

At 08:00 AM, the sensor measures an oxygen percentage of 21.2 and stores it in a variable named oxygen_level.

At 12:00 PM, after a spacewalk airlock cycle, the oxygen level dips slightly to 19.8. The astronaut logs this new value into oxygen_level.

The mission director needs an alert banner displayed on the terminal using an f-string:

Current Station Oxygen: 19.8%

Your Task:

Create oxygen_level = 21.2.

Update oxygen_level = 19.8.

Print the alert banner using an f-string to match the expected output.

1.5 Data Type
Introduction to Data Types
In real life, different items serve different purposes. You can wear a jacket, but you can't drink it. You can drink a glass of water, but you can't wear it!
Computers work the exact same way. When you give information to Python, it needs to know what kind of data it is so it knows what it is allowed to do with it.
For example:
You can do math with numbers (like 10 + 5 = 15).
But you can’t subtract a pet's name from a shoe size!
In Python, the category or form of data you give to a variable is called its Data Type.
Click Next Lesson to discover the four most important data types every coder uses!
List of Data Types
Python has four primary building-block data types that you'll use constantly:
Click Next Lesson to see these four data types in action!
Example: Checking Data Types
Let's create one variable for each data type:
Output
Cool Python Secret:
If you ever want Python to tell you the data type of any variable, wrap it in the type() function:
Click Next Lesson to test your knowledge with a quiz!
Quiz: Spot the Float
Which of the following values is treated as a float (floating-point number) in Python?
Tap an option below to answer:
Incorrect, give it another shot! 42 is a whole number without a decimal point, making it an integer (int).
Incorrect, give it another shot! Because 3.14 is wrapped inside quotation marks, Python treats it as a string (str), not a number!

Correct Answer! 🎉
Even though .0 has zero value after the decimal, the presence of the decimal point makes it a floating-point number (float).
D: True
Incorrect, give it another shot! True is a boolean (bool), which represents a true/false condition.
Quiz: The Quote Trap
Look at this line of code:
What is the data type of the variable goals?
Tap an option below to answer:

A: int (Integer)
Incorrect, give it another shot! Look closely at the quotation marks around "10". Quotation marks always turn values into text.

B: str (String)
Correct Answer! 🎉
Any value enclosed in quotation marks " " is always recognized as a string (str) by Python.

C: float
Incorrect, give it another shot! A float must have a decimal point and must not be enclosed in quotes.
D: bool
Incorrect, give it another shot! Booleans can only be True or False.
Practice: Wildlife Sanctuary Animal Profile
Problem Description
Create a profile card for a cheetah living in a wildlife reserve:
Create a string variable animal with the value "Cheetah".
Create an integer variable speed_kmh with the value 110.
Create a float variable weight_kg with the value 52.4.
Create a boolean variable is_wild with the value True.
Print all four variables on separate lines in that order.
Hints:
Do not put quotes around speed_kmh, weight_kg, or is_wild.
True must have a capital T without quotation marks.
Example:
Practice: Science Lab Sensor Reading
Problem Description
A student is recording an experiment in a chemistry lab:
Create a variable chemical and assign it the string "Distilled Water".
Create a variable ph_level and assign it the float value 7.0.
Create a variable test_number and assign it the integer value 3.

Use a single print() statement with commas to display all three values with labels:
Chemical: Distilled Water pH: 7.0 Test: 3
Example:
Scenario-Based Question: Mars Exploration Rover
Scenario:
NASA's engineering team is preparing the telemetry readout for a new Mars rover called Curiosity-II. The dashboard computer needs to display the rover's initial launch statistics.
Here is the telemetry data:
Rover Name: "Curiosity-II" (String)
Days in Orbit: 180 (Integer)
Battery Voltage: 28.6 (Float)
Solar Panels Deployed: True (Boolean)
Your Task:
Create variables for all four telemetry values with descriptive names: rover_name, days_in_orbit, battery_voltage, and solar_active.
Use f-strings to display the dashboard in two lines:
Line 1: Rover: Curiosity-II | Mission Days: 180
Line 2: Voltage: 28.6V | Solar Active: True
Hints:
print(f"Rover: {rover_name} | Mission Days: {days_in_orbit}")
print(f"Voltage: {battery_voltage}V | Solar Active: {solar_active}")
Example:

1.6  Arithmetic Operators

Operators Introduction

Welcome to your computer's calculator engine! ⚡

Until now, we’ve used Python to store and display information. But computers became famous because they can do millions of calculations in a split second.

To do math, Python uses special symbols called operators.

Think of an operator as a math tool:

The numbers you work on are called operands.

The symbol that tells Python what to do is the operator.

For example, in 8 + 4, 8 and 4 are operands, and + is the operator!

Click Next Lesson to meet the core arithmetic operators.

Arithmetic Operators

Arithmetic operators handle all the everyday math calculations you learn in school:

Let’s explore them one by one! Click Next Lesson to start with addition.

+ Operator

You can also chain multiple values: total = 10 + 20 + 35.

Print Operators (Addition)

1.7 Getting user Input

User Input Intro
Until now, our programs have had all their values pre-written inside the code. But real apps aren’t static—they talk to you!
Search engines ask what you want to search for.
Games ask for your character’s name.
Calculator apps ask for the numbers you want to add.
When a program asks a human for information while running, that information is called user input.
With user input, your programs become alive, interactive, and personalized!
Click Next Lesson to learn how to make your computer ask questions!
Take User Input
In Python, we collect information from the keyboard using the input() function.
You can put a friendly prompt message inside the parentheses:
Sample Interaction
How It Works:
1.  Python prints Enter astronaut name: and pauses.
2.  It waits for the user to type something on the keyboard and press the Enter key.
3.  Whatever the user types is saved directly into the variable pilot_name!
Practice: Robot Welcome Message
Problem Description
Write a program that asks for the user's favorite hobby and prints an excited message.
1.  Use input("What is your favorite hobby? ") and store the answer in a variable named hobby.
2.  Print: That sounds awesome! I want to try followed by their hobby.
Example:
Use input() With Numbers
Here is a super important rule that every coder must remember:
The input() function ALWAYS returns text (a string), even if the user types digits!
Look at what happens if you try to do math with raw input:
Output
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
Because age is stored as the string "12" instead of the number 12, Python cannot add 1 to it!
The Solution:
Convert the string into an integer using int() or into a float using float():
Sample Output
A General Tip: Convert in One Step
Instead of taking two lines to ask and then convert, professional Python coders combine them into one neat line:
Here, input() gets the text from the user, and int() or float() converts it immediately before saving it into your variable!
Quiz: What Does input() Return?
Look at this line of code:
If the user types 500 and presses Enter, what is the data type stored inside score?
Tap an option below to answer:
A: int (Integer)
Incorrect, give it another shot! input() never creates integers automatically, even if the user only types digits. |
B: float
Incorrect, give it another shot! input() does not convert values to decimals on its own. |
C: str (String)

Correct Answer! 🎉
input() always captures keyboard input as a string (str). If the user types 500, it is saved as "500".
D: bool
Incorrect, give it another shot! input() never produces boolean values directly. |

1.8 Type Conversion

Intro to Type Conversion

In coding, data doesn't always arrive in the exact form you need.

A user types the number 25, but Python hands it to you as the text string "25".

A stopwatch measures a race time of 14.8 seconds, but your leaderboard only awards whole-second points.

When you transform data from one data type into another, it is called Type Conversion (or data type transformation).

It's like melting ice into liquid water: the core information is still there, but its state has changed so you can use it in a brand-new way!

Click Next Lesson to learn the two ways Python converts data.

Type Casting vs Type Coercion

There are two distinct ways data types change in Python:

Type Coercion (Implicit / Automatic):

Python does the work for you automatically behind the scenes.

You don’t write any special conversion commands.

Example: When you add an integer and a float, Python quietly upgrades the integer to a float so no decimal precision is lost.

Type Casting (Explicit / Manual):

You specifically command Python to change the data type using conversion functions like int(), float(), or str().

Example: Converting text input into a number using int("50").

Click Next Lesson to see automatic conversion in action!

Implicit Type Conversion

Look at what happens when you combine an integer with a float:

Output

How It Works

Python automatically promotes 4 into 4.0 before performing the addition. It does this to make sure your answer keeps its decimal accuracy without you having to lift a finger!

Quiz: Implicit Conversion Check

What will be the data type and output of result in this code?

Tap an option below to answer:

| A: 12 (int) |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! When adding an integer and a float, Python converts the result to a float to protect precision. |

| B: 12.0 (float) |
| Correct Answer! 🎉
Python automatically coerces score to 10.0, resulting in a floating-point sum of 12.0. |

| C: "12.0" (string) |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Mathematical operations between numbers never produce text strings. |

| D: A TypeError occurs. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Python seamlessly adds integers and floats together. |

Convert Integer (Explicit int())

When you want to convert values into whole numbers yourself, you use the int() function.

You simply place whatever you want to convert inside its parentheses:

Output

In computer logic, True corresponds to 1 (switch ON) and False corresponds to 0 (switch OFF)!

Practice: Boolean to Integer Status

Problem Description

A smart security light has two sensor states:

door_open = False

Convert both boolean variables to integers using int() and print them on separate lines.

Hints:

print(int(motion_detected))

print(int(door_open))

Example:

Converting Floats to Integers

When you pass a floating-point number into int(), something very specific happens:

Python simply chops off (truncates) the decimal part completely! It does NOT round to the nearest number.

Output

Notice that even though 14.99 is practically 15, int() doesn't care about rounding—it simply discards .99 and leaves only the whole number 14.

Quiz: Chopping the Decimals

| A: 13 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! , but Python converts each float before adding them! |

| B: 12 |
| Correct Answer! 🎉
 int(9.8) truncates to 9, and int(3.2) truncates to 3. ! |

| C: 13.0 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Adding two integers always produces an integer, not a float. |

| D: 12.0 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Both values were converted to integers first, so no decimal is printed. |

Practice: Full Laps Completed

Problem Description: A drone completed 8.75 laps around an obstacle course before its battery ran low.

Create a variable total_laps = 8.75.

Convert total_laps to a whole integer using int() to find the number of fully completed laps, and store it in full_laps.

Print: Full laps completed: followed by full_laps.

Example:

Converting Numeric Strings to Integers

You can also convert text strings into numbers, as long as the text contains only valid whole numbers:

Output

Watch Out For ValueErrors:

If the string contains letters or a decimal point, int() will crash with an error!

int("Hello") ❌ ValueError (not a number!)

int("45.6") ❌ ValueError (has a decimal! To convert "45.6", you must use float("45.6") first).

Quiz: Valid String Conversion

Which of the following string conversions will run successfully without an error?

Tap an option below to answer:

| A: int("Twenty-Five") |

| Incorrect, give it another shot! English word numbers cannot be read by int(). Only numeric digits work. |

| B: int("100") |

| Correct Answer! 🎉

"100" contains only digits representing a whole number, so int() converts it into 100 cleanly. |

| C: int("50.5") |

| Incorrect, give it another shot! int() cannot directly convert a string with a decimal point. It raises a ValueError. |

| D: int("12A") |

| Incorrect, give it another shot! The letter A prevents Python from reading it as a pure base-10 number. |

Practice: Ticket Sales Calculation

Problem Description

A museum kiosk received two ticket orders stored as text strings:

morning_tickets = "14"

afternoon_tickets = "26"

Convert both strings to integers using int(), add them together to calculate total_tickets, and print total_tickets.

At an amusement arcade, players earn game points on their digital cards.

A player scanned their card, and the machine returned their points as a float: raw_points = 248.85.

At the prize counter, tickets are only awarded for full, whole points (the arcade chops off any decimal fractions).

Each prize costs 50 tickets.

Your Task:

Create raw_points = 248.85.

Convert raw_points into an integer named tickets using int().

Calculate how many prizes the player can claim using floor division //: prizes = tickets // 50.

Calculate leftover tickets using modulo %: leftover = tickets % 50.

Revision & Summary: Chapter 1 Master Checklist

Congratulations! 🏆 You have completed the foundational core of Python!

Here is your master cheat-sheet for everything you’ve mastered:

Output (print): Displays text and calculations. Use commas , for spaces or \n for line breaks.

Modern Formatting (f-strings): Combine variables and words cleanly: f"Hello {name}!".

Comments (#): Human notes that Python skips.

Variables: Labeled storage boxes for data. Reassign values with = or swap using a helper temp.

Data Types:

int: Whole numbers (10, -3)

float: Decimals (3.14, 0.5)

str: Text in quotes ("Python")

bool: True/False logic switches

Arithmetic Operators: +, -, *, / (always float), // (quotient), % (remainder), ** (powers).

User Input (input()): Collects user responses from the keyboard as strings by default.

Type Conversion:

Implicit (Coercion): Python automatically converts int + float into float.

Explicit (Casting): Use int(), float(), or str() to manually change data types.

You are now 100% ready to move on to Chapter 2: Making Decisions (Conditionals & Logic)!

1.10 Revision
Revision 1 (Output, Comments & Variables)
Welcome to your grand review! Let’s revisit the foundational coding blocks you unlocked in the first half of this module:
1. Displaying Output (print())
print("message"): Sends text to the screen. Text must always be inside quotation marks " ".
Multiple Values with Commas: print("Level:", 5) puts a neat space between each item.
Newline (\n): Acts like pressing the Enter key: print("Line 1\nLine 2").
Triple Quotes ("""..."""): Keeps long paragraphs and art formatted across multiple lines.
2. Comments (#)
Starts with #: print("Hello") # This is a human note.
Python completely ignores comments. Use them to make your code clear, readable, and easy to understand.
3. Variables
Labeled boxes that hold data in computer memory using =: player_name = "Kiran".
Updating Variables: Variables only hold one value at a time; assigning a new value replaces the old one.
Swapping Variables: To swap two variables without losing data, always use a third helper variable (temp).

input("prompt"): Pauses and waits for the user to type on the keyboard. Always returns a string!
